pharm: Bactericidal aminoglycoside that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis; poorly absorbed from the GI tract so used orally to suppress gut flora, but the small absorbed fraction can cause nephro-, oto-, and neurotoxicity.
quick: Hepatic coma 4-12 g/day in divided doses for 5-6 days; bowel prep per regimen with erythromycin
Oral; bowel-prep regimens are given around a clear-liquid/low-residue diet
Aminoglycosides can cause fetal harm (congenital deafness reported); avoid unless essential
Caution; aminoglycosides may pass into milk - poorly absorbed orally by infant
Greatly increased nephro-/ototoxicity risk; reduce dose or stop if renal insufficiency develops
Used in hepatic coma but accumulates; monitor for toxicity, watch serum levels
Renal function, serial audiometry and vestibular tests, neomycin serum levels
summary: Oral neomycin sulfate is a poorly absorbed aminoglycoside used as adjunctive therapy to suppress bowel flora (preoperative colorectal preparation, given with erythromycin) and as adjunctive treatment of hepatic coma by reducing ammonia-forming intestinal bacteria. It carries a BOXED WARNING: systemic absorption occurs after oral use and can cause neurotoxicity (including permanent bilateral ototoxicity), nephrotoxicity, and neuromuscular blockade with respiratory paralysis - even at recommended doses and even with normal renal function at higher/longer dosing. Risk rises with renal impairment, prolonged therapy, and concurrent other nephro/neurotoxic drugs. Use the lowest dose for the shortest time (treatment beyond two weeks is not recommended). It is contraindicated in intestinal obstruction and in inflammatory/ulcerative GI disease.
indications: Suppression of normal intestinal bacterial flora, e.g., preoperative preparation of the bowel (given with erythromycin)
Adjunctive therapy of hepatic coma (portal-systemic encephalopathy) by reducing ammonia-forming intestinal bacteria

dosage.d: 4 to 12 g/day of neomycin sulfate (8-24 tablets) in divided doses for 5-6 days; up to 4 g/day for chronic insufficiency
dosage.n: Withdraw dietary protein, avoid diuretics, give supportive therapy; monitor for toxicity and serum levels

dosage.d: 1 g neomycin with 1 g erythromycin base at 1 pm, 2 pm, and 11 pm on the day before an 8 am surgery (after appropriate diet/laxative prep)
dosage.n: Part of a multi-day mechanical bowel preparation regimen

dosage.d: Use the lowest possible dose for the shortest possible period
dosage.n: Treatment for periods longer than two weeks is not recommended

admin: Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible duration to minimize toxicity
Do not treat for longer than two weeks
Perform serial renal function, audiometric, and vestibular testing, especially in high-risk patients
Monitor neomycin serum concentrations during hepatic-coma dosing to avoid toxic levels
Avoid concurrent or sequential other aminoglycosides and nephro/neurotoxic drugs (e.g., bacitracin, cisplatin, vancomycin, amphotericin B, polymyxin B, colistin, viomycin)
moa: Neomycin is a bactericidal aminoglycoside that acts by binding to the bacterial ribosome and inhibiting protein synthesis in susceptible cells. It is effective primarily against gram-negative bacilli (e.g., Escherichia coli, the Klebsiella-Enterobacter group) and is not active against anaerobic bowel flora. Given orally, it is poorly absorbed and rapidly suppresses intestinal bacterial growth for 48-72 hours; in hepatic coma this reduces ammonia-forming bacteria and lowers blood ammonia.

absolute: History of hypersensitivity to neomycin (or cross-sensitivity to other aminoglycosides)
Inflammatory or ulcerative gastrointestinal disease (risk of enhanced absorption)
relative: Concurrent anesthetics or neuromuscular blocking agents
monitor: Signs of neuromuscular blockade / respiratory depression

preg: Aminoglycosides can cause fetal harm; they cross the placenta and total irreversible bilateral congenital deafness has been reported with streptomycin in pregnancy. If neomycin is used during pregnancy or the patient becomes pregnant, advise her of the potential hazard to the fetus.
lact: Use with caution in nursing women. Note the risk of ototoxicity in carriers of certain mitochondrial 12S rRNA (MT-RNR1, e.g., m.1555A>G) variants; orally administered aminoglycoside is poorly absorbed by the infant.
renal: The risk of nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity is greater in renal impairment. Small amounts of oral neomycin are absorbed; if renal insufficiency develops during therapy, reduce the dose or discontinue. Neomycin can be removed by hemodialysis.
hepatic: Used as adjunctive therapy in hepatic coma; however, the drug accumulates and the benefit must be weighed against nephro-/oto-toxicity and neuromuscular blockade. Monitor frequently for toxicity and check serum levels.

major: Other aminoglycosides / nephrotoxic-ototoxic drugs (bacitracin, cisplatin, vancomycin, amphotericin B, polymyxin B, colistin, viomycin) - additive toxicity; avoid
Neuromuscular blocking agents and anesthetics (tubocurarine, succinylcholine, decamethonium) - potentiated neuromuscular blockade and respiratory paralysis
Potent diuretics (e.g., ethacrynic acid, furosemide) - enhanced ototoxicity
moderate: Oral anticoagulants (warfarin) - neomycin may enhance anticoagulant effect (reduced vitamin K absorption)
Massive transfusion of citrate-anticoagulated blood - additive neuromuscular blockade risk
minor: Oral cyanocobalamin (vitamin B12), and absorption of fat, glucose, xylose, lactose, cholesterol, carotene, sodium, calcium, iron - reduced by high-dose neomycin (malabsorption syndrome)
interactions.food: High-dose oral neomycin (about 12 g/day) produces a malabsorption syndrome.
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction described in the label.
interactions.diagnostics: May reduce absorption of orally administered drugs and nutrients; can lower serum cholesterol.

common: Malabsorption syndrome with prolonged therapy (increased fecal fat, decreased serum carotene, reduced xylose absorption)
rare: Numbness, skin tingling, muscle twitching, convulsions (additional neurotoxicity)
emergency: Sudden or progressive deafness (may be delayed in onset)

monitoring: Serial renal function tests (especially high-risk patients)
Neomycin serum concentrations during hepatic-coma dosing
Signs of neuromuscular blockade and respiratory depression
Vitamin B12 / nutrient status with prolonged use
counsel: Take this antibiotic exactly as directed and only for the time prescribed - long courses raise the risk of serious harm
Tell your doctor right away about hearing changes, ringing in the ears, dizziness, or balance problems - these can be permanent
Report reduced urination or swelling, which may signal kidney problems
Report severe muscle weakness or trouble breathing immediately
This medicine treats bacteria; it will not work for viral illnesses, and misuse promotes resistance
pk: Suppresses gut bacterial growth promptly after oral dosing
Poorly absorbed orally (~3% absorbed); ~97% eliminated unchanged in feces
About 2-3 hours for the absorbed fraction (longer in renal impairment); tissue-bound drug released slowly over weeks
Suppression of intestinal flora persists 48-72 hours
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); dispense in tight containers
pearls: BOXED WARNING: even oral neomycin is absorbed enough to cause nephrotoxicity, permanent ototoxicity, and neuromuscular blockade/respiratory paralysis
Ototoxicity may be delayed and irreversible - hearing loss can develop after the drug is stopped
Use the lowest dose for the shortest time; do not exceed 2 weeks of therapy
Avoid stacking with other aminoglycosides, loop diuretics, or nephro/neurotoxic drugs
Contraindicated in intestinal obstruction and in inflammatory/ulcerative bowel disease (enhanced absorption)
missed: If a scheduled dose is missed during a fixed bowel-prep or hepatic-coma regimen, contact the prescriber - timing within these regimens matters; do not double the dose.
overdose: Acute overdose is unlikely because of poor absorption, but prolonged administration can produce systemic levels causing neurotoxicity, ototoxicity, and/or nephrotoxicity. Discontinue the drug; hemodialysis will remove neomycin from the blood. For neuromuscular blockade, calcium salts may reverse the effect but mechanical ventilation may be required.
